summary:
SALUS is an interactive health monitoring prototype that helps astronauts check their health and decide what to share with their crew medical responder. During long missions, sleep and other health indicators can change, and getting timely medical advice from Earth can be harder.

Astronauts use an interactive body map to choose a concern, follow a guided self-assessment, and see how their readings compare with their own history. SALUS uses a machine learning model called Isolation Forest to flag unusual patterns in sleep duration and resting heart rate for review. If an astronaut reports an urgent warning sign, the app pauses the check-in and shows who to alert.

The prototype uses 480 fictional daily records to demonstrate the workflow. Research from NASA’s Human Research Program appears alongside the results, with links to the original sources. SALUS gives the crew a way to turn a concern into a clear record of what they felt, what changed, and what to do next.
details:
I built SALUS, a web prototype that helps astronauts assess their health and prepare clear information for their crew medical responder. On long missions, getting medical advice from Earth can take longer. SALUS gives the crew a way to record a concern, see what has changed, and understand the next step.

An astronaut selects a concern through an interactive body map and follows a guided check-in with instructions for taking measurements. The results show their current readings alongside their personal baseline. A shared machine learning model called Isolation Forest flags unusual patterns in sleep duration and resting heart rate for review. When an astronaut reports an urgent warning sign, a separate rule pauses the routine check-in and shows who to alert.

I designed SALUS around each astronaut’s own history. The prototype uses the first 30 days of each fictional crew member’s records to establish a baseline and leaves skipped measurements blank. It also uses TF-IDF text search to display relevant NASA research summaries and source links alongside the results. I used 480 synthetic daily records to demonstrate the workflow. Clinical validation would require authorized flight data and review by medical and mission specialists.

I used Figma for interface design, React, TypeScript, and Vite for the frontend, and Python, FastAPI, SQLite, and scikit-learn for the backend and machine learning. The current prototype accepts manually entered readings in a web browser.
